Solar cells that send data

Driven with current, a solar cell gives off light like a large LED. The lab is testing whether a satellite or rover could blink its solar panels to send data if its radio fails. I owned integration and testing on the space-grade cell side: the boards and housings that hold the cells, the light source used for early link tests, and the bench setup.

Solar-cell interface boards and E26 housing

KiCad · Fusion 360 · FDM printing

The test cells needed a standard way to be powered and positioned. I designed two interface boards and a printed housing that lets a cell screw into an ordinary E26 light socket.

What I did

  • Laid out a two-layer board for the space-grade cell, sized to replace its existing carrier. Three front pads take the cell's clip contacts (GND, PV+, GND); two large back pads take the socket leads; vias carry power between them on 1.5 mm traces.
  • Laid out a second board that holds two small cells in parallel. Its 2 × 2 mm pads match the gold contacts on the back of each cell, so the cells sit straight on the board.
  • Modeled the housing in Fusion 360 as a square-to-round loft that sits on the E26 adapter collar, with a pocket that holds the board flush, then printed and fit-tested it.
Board and housing specs
Large board
71 × 50 mm, 2 layers
Front pads
3 × 11 × 6 mm, 14 mm pitch
Back pads

Small board

Problems and fixes

Problem

The first housing print was too tight. The board would not seat in the pocket.

Fix

Measured the print against the board, opened up the pocket, and reprinted. The second print seated the board and the adapter.

Problem

A board off by a millimetre will not meet the cell's contacts, and a fab run takes days.

Fix

Printed the layout on paper at 1:1, laid it on the real cell, and adjusted the outline and pads until they matched before ordering.

Turning a stage light into a data transmitter

Python · FTDI D2XX · DMX512 · photodiode · oscilloscope

To test optical data links before the solar-cell transmitter was ready, the lab used a 14-channel DMX stage light as a stand-in. It came with no manual, and no driver worked with our adapter. I got it under computer control, made its flash rate accurate, and used it to send bytes of data.

What I did

  • Reverse-engineered the fixture's 14-channel map by stepping each channel and watching what the light did.
  • Drove a bare FT232R USB adapter directly through the FTDI D2XX API (ftd2xx): 250 kbaud, 8 data bits, 2 stop bits, hardware break.
  • Measured real flash rates with a photodiode and oscilloscope instead of trusting the command.
  • Built frequency-shift keying on top: 30 Hz for a 0, 70 Hz for a 1, a quarter second per bit and a half-second dark gap per byte. The light is forced off briefly at each bit boundary so every bit has a clean edge.
  • Sent a counting test and decoded the recording back to 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, the sequence that was sent.
  • Wrote a setup guide with photos, the channel map and a troubleshooting table, so the next student can rebuild it from a blank computer.
Link specs
Fixture
14-channel DMX512
Interface
FT232R, 250 kbaud, 8N2
Verified range
2.5–100 Hz
Rate jitter
~24% → ~2%
Commanded
40 / 60 / 100 Hz
Measured
41.0 / 60.3 / 100.5 Hz
FSK
30 Hz = 0, 70 Hz = 1
Byte timing
2.09 s + 0.51 s gap

Problems and fixes

Problem

Two open-source DMX libraries failed: one was Linux-only, the other expected an Enttec PRO interface, not a bare FTDI chip.

Fix

Wrote the DMX framing myself on the D2XX API, including the line settings and the hardware break.

Problem

Slow-motion phone video gave 11, 4 and 3.6 Hz for the same strobe setting. The camera's frame rate was aliasing the flashes.

Fix

Switched to a photodiode on the oscilloscope and filtered out the LED's internal PWM.

Problem

Python's time.sleep() gave about 24% jitter, and the flash rate fell behind the command above 60 Hz.

Fix

Replaced it with busy-wait timing. Jitter dropped to about 2%, and the rate tracks the command up to 100 Hz.

Problem

The first decode attempt recorded a 0.2 s window, shorter than a single bit.

Fix

Recorded 18 s instead, enough for several full bytes, and decoded from that.

CubeSat panel PCB and tripod tray

KiCad · Fusion 360 · FDM printing

For testing, the cells ride on a CubeSat frame. I laid out the panel board that bolts to the frame and designed the printed tray that holds the frame on a camera tripod.

What I did

  • Compared against the old board to find the bolt positions, then checked them in the real frame.
  • Set the design up as one solar panel per board, mounted on two sides of the frame, and moved the connectors to line up with the metal framing on the back.
  • Redesigned the tripod holder to slip over the tripod's stud instead of using a screw mount.
Problem

The tray's corner brackets covered the edges of the cells.

Fix

Shortened the brackets so they locate the frame without shading the panels.

Problem

One center socket carries the whole CubeSat, so the tray could flex when the frame was mounted.

Fix

Added hollow ribs from the socket out to the floor: stiffer, but still light.

Lab bench work

The day-to-day work that kept the project moving. The receiver and modulator boards are the lab's existing designs; I assembled and tested them.

Receiver test

Ran the photodiode detector into the scope over BNC, then tested it in a dark room with a flashlight to confirm it responds to light.

Modulator board assembly

Soldered the lab's EL modulator board, which drives the solar cell and adds external on/off switching: op-amps, MOSFETs and screw-terminal connectors.

Light-output measurements

Drove the cell in forward bias from a current-limited bench supply and measured its emission with a spectrometer and integrating sphere. Wrote a MATLAB script to integrate the spectra and checked it against the vendor software.

Parts and BOMs

Sorted the lab's parts stock, checked it against the BOMs of three boards, and ordered what was missing. Built a MOSFET table ranked by gate threshold voltage.

Spectrometer driver

Traced a dead spectrometer to a Windows driver-policy block (Device Manager Code 39, CodeIntegrity Event 3077). The vendor confirmed the cause.

Reflective coating

Looked into Prof. Xiulin Ruan's 98%-reflectance barium-sulfate paint for the printed parts, to push more light toward the sensor.

LiDAR terrain scanner

Arduino Nano · TF Mini LiDAR · nRF24L01 · Fusion 360 · Processing

A pan-tilt scanner that sweeps a TF Mini LiDAR across a scene and radios each point to a laptop, which draws a 3D point cloud as the scan runs. It was built to map underwater terrain from above the surface. Published with my mentor in IJSHRE.

What I did

  • Designed the two-servo pan-tilt mount in Fusion 360 and printed it, balancing the sensor and servos around the axes.
  • Built the scanner on an Arduino Nano, with a resistor divider for the sensor's 3.3 V logic and an nRF24L01 radio.
  • Built the ground station on Veroboard: a second Nano and radio that pass each point to the laptop over USB serial.
  • Wrote the plotting code that turns pan angle, tilt angle and range into a 3D point cloud you can rotate.
  • Tested in a lit room, a dark room and daylight, then over a tub of water with sand and blocks on the bottom.

Problems and fixes

Problem

The first mount was built around full-size metal-gear servos, which made it bulky.

Fix

Redesigned the mount for 9 g micro servos.

Problem

Ambient light saturated the sensor, and scans got noisier the higher it sat above the water.

Fix

Scanned in low light and kept the sensor close to the surface, where the bottom came through most clearly.

Modular prosthetic forearm

Fusion 360 · FDM printing · laser cutting · user interviews

A low-cost, 3D-printed forearm for arm amputees. One socket takes interchangeable attachments, a claw, a two-finger gripper or a ring, held by a twist-and-key lock the wearer can change without help.

Status: printed and assembled; not yet tested by a wearer.

What I did

  • Sketched five concepts and scored them on aesthetics, audience, materials, size, user needs and function. The activity-specific attachment design scored 17 of 20.
  • Interviewed an arm amputee, who ranked the same design first and pointed out that the most natural-looking hand was also the least useful.
  • Sized the forearm from anthropometric data, using the 50th-percentile forearm length of 23.3 cm.
  • Built test models to try joints, attachments and socket fit, including a Styrofoam forearm to check strength and weight.
  • Modeled the final forearm, lock and attachments in Fusion 360 and printed them.
Problem

The 180° rotating joint limited which attachments would work, and attachments could work loose and break it.

Fix

Replaced it with a four-lug twist lock and key: turn the attachment, key it, and it stays put.

Problem

The first printed socket was too narrow and hard to wear comfortably.

Fix

Modeled a separate insert to line and pad the socket.
